On October 20th, SpaceX reported monster Q3 earnings, with revenue up over 160% from a year ago, but only 12% of that came from rockets. Over 50% of it came from SpaceX's burgeoning AI business, and Elon made jaw-dropping revenue projections off the back of it during the earnings call.

> **Elon Musk:** "...somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion. ... on that crazy note, I thought..."
>
> **SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell:** "On that crazy note."

*SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call, October 20th, 2026*

But that isn't all. He also predicted a slew of failures across the neoclouds, the companies that rent out AI chips, and said he'd closed a landmark $40 billion debt deal to fund his data center ambitions. So are these projections realistic, or is this just a ploy to build hype for the company?

## AI Overtakes Starlink

A year ago, Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet business, was over half of its revenue, rockets were about 30%, and AI was about 15%. This quarter, AI is 52%, Starlink is 36%, and rockets are just 12%. So in a year, AI went from the smallest of SpaceX's three businesses to the biggest.

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="ai-overtakes-starlink" />

But the rocket revenue isn't shrinking. Customers paid SpaceX $1.8 billion for its rocket business, up 6% from a year ago. It flew 35 launches, most of them for Starlink, and Starship, its giant next-generation rocket that Elon built to eventually go to Mars, reached orbit for the first time on its 14th flight.

Starlink brought in $5.2 billion, up about 70% from a year ago, and it now has 13.6 million consumer subscribers. It's also making a big push into phone service: more than 22 million people a month already use it on their phones, and it plans to become a carrier itself, competing with the likes of Verizon.

But the real story was the growth in the AI business.

AI brought in $7.6 billion, more than nine times what it made a year ago, which makes it bigger than Starlink for the first time. SpaceX's AI business is multifaceted. It includes multiple different businesses, including Grok and X subscriptions, as well as revenue from Cursor, the AI coding company they bought for $60 billion in stock earlier this year. But the lion's share of that revenue came from SpaceX's monster AI compute business, which essentially involves SpaceX renting out data centers to AI labs and hyperscalers, the giant cloud companies. Just this year they've signed deals with Anthropic and Google, and the business is growing at an explosive pace, with about $6.4 billion this quarter alone, together with those Grok and X subscriptions (SpaceX doesn't split them out).

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="the-quarter" />

And it's supposed to get a lot bigger.

## 13 Gigawatts

> "I would be surprised if we brought on less than 13 GW of compute by the end of next year."

*Elon Musk, on the call*

For context, a gigawatt is the main unit used to measure AI compute businesses, and represents the amount of computing power you have to sell. SpaceX had 1.7 gigawatts at the end of September, and it wants 2.5 to 3 by December. That's a blistering pace. CoreWeave, one of the biggest AI clouds, had about 1.5 gigawatts running in total at the end of June. But Elon says SpaceX has an unfair advantage given their engineering prowess.

> "This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It's not fair."

And he does have a point. They are literally rocket scientists. But computers on their own aren't revenue. So how does a gigawatt actually turn into money? Companies rent out the compute, and SpaceX prices it on a per watt basis. So let's say you're OpenAI or Anthropic, and you need more capacity to run your models so you can generate more revenue. You strike a deal with SpaceX, or one of the AI clouds, and pay for the watts you use.

So ultimately, the revenue comes down to two numbers: how many gigawatts SpaceX has, and the price per watt.

On the last call, in August, Elon guessed SpaceX could charge somewhere between $30 and $50 a watt, which we read as a year's rent. So one gigawatt at $30 a watt is about $30 billion a year. At $50, it's about $50 billion. Now do that thirteen times. On our math, 13 gigawatts at $50 a watt is about $650 billion a year. That's also where Elon's revenue speculation from earlier came from.

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="the-formula" />

> "In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of '27 is somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion."

One catch: Elon plans to rent about half of it out and keep the other half for SpaceX's own AI. That half doesn't pay rent; it earns through Grok. But on our math, his range only works if every gigawatt is available for external consumption.

But SpaceX doesn't set that price the way most AI clouds do. Most AI clouds rent their chips out like apartments. They sign customers to multi-year leases at a fixed price. SpaceX's deals can be ended on short notice, so it rents more like a hotel, and its best-known guest is Anthropic. Anthropic's own IPO filing, out in October, shows it has agreed to spend up to $120.5 billion with SpaceX's AI arm, about $3.1 billion a month once it's all switched on in December. On our math, that alone would be more than a third of the $100 billion a year pace SpaceX's CFO wants the whole company at by then. But the same filing shows that from early 2027, either side can walk away on 90 days' notice.

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="the-hotel" />

These short-term arrangements are known as renting at the spot price, which is just today's going rate, not a price locked in for years. And on the call, Elon explained why he does it this way.

> "Our approach is to rent at effectively the spot-market rate, as opposed to signing these long-term deals ... I think the smart move is to do short-term contracts and essentially to place the bet on useful intelligence per watt increasing rapidly."

So far, prices are going his way, and he says those short contracts are coming up for renewal at higher prices.

> "We see them renewing at higher dollars per watt, not lower dollars per watt."

And it's not just his word. On the Ornn Compute Price Index, which tracks what renting a chip actually costs, Nvidia's B200 rented for $9.77 an hour on October 30th, up about a fifth in a month.

SpaceX's CFO says pricing is now slightly above the top of that $30 to $50 range, and at today's prices, every new batch of computers pays for itself in under a year. And Elon says there's more demand than he can supply, stating: "We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone."

So SpaceX has the formula, the prices and the demand. But can this really get to $1 trillion in run rate?

## Does the Trillion Add Up?

Let's run Elon's trillion backwards, with the same formula.

Quick note first: every number in this section is a run rate. That's what SpaceX would bring in over a year at its pace at the end of 2027, December's revenue times twelve. It's not what SpaceX actually books in 2027.

Take the top of his own price range, $50 a watt. To hit $1 trillion, SpaceX would need 20 gigawatts of capacity available for external consumption. And at the end of September, it had 1.7.

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="run-backwards" />

So we built three cases of our own. Depending on how much SpaceX builds and what it can charge, they run anywhere from about $120 billion to the full trillion.

| Case | Gigawatts | Price per watt, per year | Run rate, end of 2027 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bear | 6 | $20 | $120 billion |
| Base | 10 | $30 | $300 billion |
| Bull | 20 | $50 | $1 trillion |

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="the-three-cases" />

And the range is that wide because both of those can swing. If rental prices keep rising, those short contracts reprice up, like a hotel raising its rates, and SpaceX heads for the bull case. If they fall, SpaceX reprices down first, and it lands in the bear case.

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="the-rate-board" />

The trillion is a long shot, but this is obviously going to become a really, really big business. It's not hard to see SpaceX reaching a $200 billion a year pace, or more, at the scale it's playing at. On our math, the likeliest landing is a run rate of about $300 billion by the end of 2027: about 10 gigawatts at around $30 a watt. 10 gigawatts is what Elon himself said in August, and it's short of the 13 he says he'd be surprised to miss. That's triple the CFO's $100 billion target, and still well short of Elon's $500 billion low end.

Whether or not he hits it, just the threat of Elon coming after this market shook up one of the hottest industries in AI.

## The Shake-Up: Guppy-Level Death

The neocloud industry makes its money the same way SpaceX's AI business does, renting out AI computing, just at a much smaller scale. Their stocks were already sliding, and then, the weekend after the call, Elon piled on.

On Saturday, October 24th, he posted that he expects "a lot of stranded compute in partially complete data centers." The next day he said the 200-plus neoclouds are going to see "guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many."

His argument, basically, is that they're undercapitalized. They borrow to buy chips and he says debt markets have "almost entirely shut off access to money" for anyone without revenue outside AI data centers, and they can't match the sheer volume SpaceX is building.

And the gap in scale is real. CoreWeave, one of the biggest neoclouds, brought in about $2.6 billion in its latest quarter. SpaceX's AI cloud and subscriptions, leaving out Cursor, brought in about $6.4 billion, roughly two and a half times as much. CoreWeave has signed up for about 3.7 gigawatts of power in total. Elon says he'd be surprised if SpaceX has less than 13 running by the end of 2027.

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="coreweave-and-spacex" />

But that raises the obvious question: if borrowing is what's sinking the guppies, how does SpaceX pay for its own build?

## How He Pays for It

Currently they are spending at a staggering rate. SpaceX spent $19.6 billion in Q3, mostly on AI data centers, which is about $10 billion more than its businesses brought in as cash. And in Q4 it expects to spend another $35 to $40 billion.

But SpaceX has a fortress balance sheet from its core businesses and recent IPO. At the end of September, it was sitting on nearly $90 billion of cash and investments.

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="the-cash" />

And unlike the guppies, SpaceX can borrow, because it's investment grade and has the Starlink cash cow business as a structural advantage. However, Elon's also tapping the private markets. The Financial Times reported that SpaceX was raising $40 billion of debt to buy GPUs, with the mammoth private equity firm Apollo expected to lead. Elon says it's closed; Bloomberg reported the same day that talks were still going on. The next day, SpaceX's own filing called it a binding commitment, with the price still to be set and the deal expected to close by year-end. Under the deal, an Apollo-managed company buys the chips and leases them to SpaceX, so the chips themselves back the money. So again, the scale Elon's created is a massive competitive advantage, and puts him in a power position to dominate the AI compute market for the foreseeable future.

<DashboardEmbed collection="spacex-q3-2026" slug="the-lease" />

## Not Just a Rocket Company

So SpaceX may still have a rocket business, but it isn't just a rocket company anymore. It's a full-blown hyperscaler that can rival anybody in the AI computing space.

Elon's trillion-dollar run rate is a long shot. But whether he gets there or not, he's betting SpaceX is the neocloud left standing.
